title: Inside the transformer: attention
blurb: How each token works out which other tokens matter to it.

slides.title: From tokens to a prediction
body: Most of today’s language models are transformers. Inside, each token is turned into a vector — a list of numbers — that then gets refined layer by layer.
Each layer updates every token’s vector using information from the others. The step that lets tokens share information is called attention.

visual.caption: Simplified view of a text-generation transformer.

items.label: Embed
items.text: Each token becomes a vector, plus information about its position.

items.label: Transform, many layers deep
items.text: Each layer updates every token’s vector using the others. Attention is the key step.

items.label: Predict
items.text: The final vector at the last position becomes a score for every token in the vocabulary.

slides.title: Attention: deciding which tokens matter
body: Take “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.” To make sense of “it”, the model needs to connect it to “animal”.
Attention lets each token give a weight to every earlier token, then mix in information from them in proportion to those weights.

visual.caption: Illustrative only. Real models have many attention “heads” per layer, each learning different patterns, and the weights are rarely this tidy.

items.heading: “animal” · strong
items.text: The most likely thing “it” refers to.

items.heading: “tired” · medium
items.text: A clue: streets don’t get tired.

items.heading: “street” · weak
items.text: Possible, but a poor fit with “tired”.

slides.title: Queries, keys and values
body: Each token’s vector is turned into three new vectors. A token’s query is compared with every earlier token’s key; better matches get higher scores.
The scores are normalised into weights that add up to 1, and the token’s new vector is the weighted mix of the values. In text generation, a token can only attend to tokens before it.

visual.caption: Each vector is produced by multiplying the token’s vector by a matrix learned in training.

items.label: Query
items.text: What this token is looking for.

items.label: Key
items.text: What each token offers, to be matched against queries.

items.label: Value
items.text: The information a token passes on when it gets attention.

slides.title: Why this design won — and its cost
body: Transformers replaced earlier designs that read text one token at a time. Attention connects any two tokens directly, and training can process every position at once.
The trade-off is cost: standard attention compares every token with every other one.

visual.caption: Many variants of attention exist to reduce the cost of long contexts.

items.heading: Parallel training
items.text: All positions in a training example are processed together, which suits modern hardware.

items.heading: Long-range links
items.text: A token can draw on any earlier token directly, however far back.

items.heading: Cost grows fast
items.text: Doubling the context roughly quadruples the attention work — one reason windows have limits.

quiz.question: What does attention let each token do?
options: Weigh and mix in information from other tokens, based on relevance
Look up its meaning in a dictionary
Skip the rest of the model
quiz.explanation: Attention computes a weight for each earlier token and combines their information accordingly.

quiz.question: In the query, key and value view, how are attention weights worked out?
options: By comparing values with other values
By comparing one token’s query with other tokens’ keys
By position only — nearer tokens always win
quiz.explanation: Query–key matches set the weights; the values are what gets mixed together using those weights.

quiz.question: Why does standard attention get expensive with long contexts?
options: Every token is compared with every other, so the work grows roughly with the square of the length
The model has to be retrained for each document
Attention only works on short text
quiz.explanation: Comparing all pairs means doubling the length roughly quadruples the work.
